abstract: |
 Accurate progesterone receptor (PR) status is a critical determinant
 of endocrine therapy eligibility in breast cancer. Although
 immunohistochemistry (IHC) remains the clinical standard,
 diagnostically ambiguous cases can exhibit substantial
 inter-pathologist variability. Pathology images alone often lack
 the molecular context needed to resolve these challenging receptor
 states, while conventional late-fusion multimodal models struggle
 to align transcriptomic information with localized histopathologic
 evidence.

 To address this challenge, we present a multimodal architecture
 integrating RNA-Seq transcriptomic profiles with whole-slide imaging.
 Our asymmetric cross-attention architecture enables each patient's
 transcriptomic profile to guide visual evidence retrieval directly
 from tissue images before slide-level aggregation, while preserving
 linear computational complexity. A Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator
 produces per-patient confidence scores that illustrate a potential
 mechanism for flagging ambiguous cases for pathologist review. A
 normalization-corrected Top-1%-Mass Concentration metric quantifies
 attention localization consistently across slides of varying size.
 In an exploratory survival analysis, a Cox model combining the
 fusion architecture with the reliability signal showed a higher
 point-estimate concordance index than clinical-only and unimodal
 baselines, though the small event count limited statistical power.

 Using the TCGA-BRCA cohort of 951 patients, the model achieved an
 ROC-AUC of 0.8482 and a PR-AUC of 0.9054. Analysis of attention
 patterns revealed significant phenotypic separation between
 PR-positive and PR-negative tumors (p = 0.018), confirming the model captures biologically meaningful spatial patterns associated with receptor status.

## Project Summary
**Dataset:** TCGA-BRCA · N = 951 patients · 638 PR+ / 313 PR-

**Stack:** PyTorch · MONAI · CHIEF ViT-B · Scikit-learn
:::

## The Challenge {#sec-challenge}

### Clinical Necessity {#sec-clinical-necessity}

PR status determines whether a breast cancer patient is a candidate
for endocrine therapies such as tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors.
A misclassification in either direction carries direct clinical cost:
false positives expose patients to ineffective hormonal therapy, while
false negatives withhold potentially curative treatment. The current
gold standard, IHC staining of biopsy tissue, is subject to inter-pathologist disagreement, particularly
in borderline cases near the positivity threshold.

### Structural Incompatibility Problem {#sec-structural-incompatibility}

The core engineering challenge is data structure, not modeling
capacity. A transcriptomic profile is a fixed-length vector occupying
an identical coordinate space across all patients. A digitized
whole-slide image yields a variable-length, unordered patch bag whose
size varies by more than an order of magnitude depending on tissue
area and scanner footprint. Standard fusion architectures address this by either compressing
the patch bag to a fixed summary, discarding spatial specificity,
or imposing positional encodings tied to scanner trajectory rather
than tissue biology. Both approaches fail to generalize across
acquisition platforms.

### Slide-Size Confounder {#sec-slide-size-confounder}

A third problem emerges not in the fusion architecture but in
evaluating it. Shannon entropy, the intuitive metric for attentional
focus, is mathematically bounded above by log N. Any interpretability
metric applied to variable-length attention distributions must be
normalized for input size before group-level conclusions can be drawn.

These three challenges motivate the architectural and measurement
design choices presented in the following sections.

## Related Work {#sec-related-work}

Prior approaches address parts of these challenges but each leaves
a critical gap.

**Attention-based MIL** [@ilse2018; @lu2021clam] operates entirely
within the visual modality, providing no mechanism for integrating
transcriptomic evidence.

**Multimodal fusion** [@chen2022pathomic] incorporates genomics but
defers the incompatibility rather than resolving it. Fusion occurs
only after the slide has been compressed into a fixed-size summary,
so the genomic signal conditions how that summary is weighted,
rather than which tissue evidence is retrieved.

**Cross-modal transformers** [@chen2021mcat] move genomic
conditioning upstream of slide-level compression but rely on
predefined gene-pathway annotations and scanner-tied positional
encodings. The slide-size confounder remains unaddressed, and no
normalization-independent interpretability metric is proposed.

Collectively, these approaches tackle individual aspects of
multimodal pathology but do not simultaneously resolve the
structural incompatibility problem, provide per-patient reliability
estimates, and support slide-size-invariant interpretation.


## Contributions {#sec-contributions}

This work introduces three components that together address the
structural, clinical triage, and interpretability gaps identified above:

**Asymmetric cross-attention fusion** treats the patient's
transcriptomic profile as a query token that searches the entire
slide for diagnostically relevant tissue at linear computational
cost, without positional encoding, pathway annotation, or
pre-aggregation.

**Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator** is a lightweight gated
fusion layer that produces a scalar confidence score reflecting
cross-modal agreement between genomic and imaging evidence.
Discordant cases are identified as candidates for pathologist review
alongside the model prediction, extending the system beyond a
discriminative score toward a potential clinical decision-support tool.

**Top-1%-Mass Concentration** is a normalization-independent
interpretability metric that quantifies attentional focus across
any slide size. It recovers statistically significant phenotypic
separation between PR- and PR+ patients that entropy-based analysis
fails to recover on the same cohort, demonstrating that the
measurement instrument rather than the model was the bottleneck.

## Proposed Framework {#sec-solution}

### Asymmetric Cross-Attention Architecture {#sec-architecture}

The approach treats the patient's transcriptomic profile as a query
and the slide as the evidence being searched. Patch-level features
come from the frozen CHIEF ViT-B encoder [@wang2024chief], pretrained
on pathology images without transcriptomic supervision and used
exclusively as a feature extractor with no weight updates on
TCGA-BRCA, preserving held-out evaluation integrity. The genomic
RNA-Seq vector is compressed from 20,513 dimensions to 512,
forming a single query token Q. Each of the N patch embeddings is
projected from 768 to 512 dimensions, forming keys K and values V.
No positional encoding is applied, preserving permutation invariance
of the unordered patch bag. Dimensionality flow through each
component is summarized in @tbl-dimensions.

| Component | Input Shape | Output Shape |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| RNA-Seq projector (Q) | (1 × 20,513) | (1 × 512) |
| Patch projector (K) | (N × 768) | (N × 512) |
| Patch projector (V) | (N × 768) | (N × 512) |
| Cross-attention | Q: (1 × 512), K/V: (N × 512) | (1 × 512) |

: Dimensionality flow through the cross-attention mechanism. {#tbl-dimensions}

The query token attends over all N patch embeddings simultaneously:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$$

Because Q has shape (1 × N) rather than (N × N), attention cost
scales linearly with slide size rather than quadratically. The output, denoted **c**, encodes the visual appearance of tissue regions the transcriptomic profile deemed most diagnostically relevant.

### Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator {#sec-gated-fusion}

The Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator estimates agreement between
the transcriptomic and visual streams on a per-patient basis. The
context vector **c** and query token **Q** are concatenated
and passed through a single linear projection with Sigmoid,
producing a scalar confidence score α ∈ (0, 1):

$$\alpha = \sigma\!\left(W_g \cdot [\mathbf{c} \Vert \mathbf{Q}] + b_g\right), \qquad
\text{gated} = \alpha \cdot \mathbf{c}$$

| Component | Input Shape | Output Shape |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Concatenation | (1 × 512), (1 × 512) | (1 × 1024) |
| Linear + Sigmoid | (1 × 1024) | scalar α ∈ (0, 1) |
| Gated output | α · c | (1 × 512) |

: Dimensionality flow through the Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator. {#tbl-dimensions-fusion}

The estimator outputs high confidence when transcriptomic and
imaging evidence point in the same direction, and low confidence
when they diverge. Note that α reflects agreement between
transcriptomic and imaging streams, not the posterior probability
that the prediction is correct. When aligned, α → 1, retaining the full
cross-attention signal. When discordant, a low raw α suppresses
the visual contribution to the final prediction, since the
transcriptomic profile has already guided which tissue regions
were retrieved at the search stage. Following Platt calibration,
cases below the empirical threshold of 0.75 would be escalated to
pathologist review in a deployed setting.

The overall architecture is shown in @fig-architecture.

![System architecture: transcriptomic profile guides visual evidence
retrieval via asymmetric cross-attention. Cases below the confidence
threshold (α < 0.75) would be escalated to pathologist review in a
deployed setting.](reports/figures/architecture.svg){#fig-architecture
fig-alt="System architecture diagram showing the asymmetric
cross-attention fusion model."}

### Top-1%-Mass Concentration Metric {#sec-concentration-metric}

The attention computation produces a weight distribution over all N
patches, extracted at inference time to quantify attentional focus.
For each patient, the top 1% of patches by attention weight are
identified; Top-1%-Mass Concentration is the fraction of total
attention mass those patches carry:

$$\text{Top-1\%-Mass} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} w_{\sigma(i)}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}$$

The denominator normalizes by total attention mass, making the
metric directly comparable across patients regardless of slide size.

![Sorted attention weight decay curves (log scale, mean ± SEM)
for PR- (red, solid) and PR+ (blue, dashed) patients on the
191-patient held-out cohort. A steeper decay indicates more
focal attention concentration; a flatter curve indicates more
distributed attention across
patches.](reports/figures/attention_spotlight.png){#fig-spotlight
fig-alt="Attention weight decay curves by PR status on a log scale."
width=100%}

## Experimental Evaluation {#sec-results}

This section reports discriminative performance against unimodal
and multimodal baselines, cross-modal reliability evaluation, and
interpretability analysis.

### Predictive Performance {#sec-model-comparison}

Four models are compared: the proposed Cross-Attention + Gate
system, Late Fusion, ABMIL, and CLAM-SB. The model was evaluated
on a stratified held-out cohort of 191 patients (80/20 split of
951 total), with 128 PR+ and 63 PR- cases reflecting the 2:1 class
imbalance of the full dataset. All results derive from inference on
trained checkpoints under identical conditions. Results are
summarized in @tbl-benchmarks.

| Model | ROC-AUC | PR-AUC | Brier Score ↓ | Input |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Cross-Attention + Gate (Ours)** | **0.8482** | **0.9054** | **0.17** | WSI + RNA-Seq |
| Late Fusion (MLP concat) | 0.7681 | 0.8968 | 0.21 | WSI + RNA-Seq |
| ABMIL [@ilse2018] | 0.7094 | 0.8060 | 0.21 | WSI only |
| CLAM-SB [@lu2021clam] | 0.6926 | 0.7735 | 0.21 | WSI only |

: Quantitative benchmarking on the 191-patient held-out cohort.
{#tbl-benchmarks}

Results resolve into two performance bands. Unimodal systems plateau
near AUC 0.69 to 0.71, unable to distinguish PR+ from PR- slides
without transcriptomic state. Late Fusion closes part of the
remaining gap, but fusion occurs after compression. The
cross-attention model applies transcriptomics at the search stage,
before compression, accounting for a +0.0801 AUC margin over Late
Fusion and +0.1388 over the best unimodal baseline
(@tbl-benchmarks, @tbl-key-results). ROC and Precision-Recall
curves are shown in @fig-roc. Weight decay regularization is
load-bearing for the base classifier; an unregularized ablation
produced a 0.37-point overfit gap (training AUC 0.9912, validation
AUC 0.6240), confirming the transcriptomic projection has sufficient
capacity to memorize labels without regularization.

The comparisons reported here are against baselines reimplemented
under identical training conditions. Published benchmarks for
PR-status classification on TCGA-BRCA exist for unimodal WSI
approaches [@lu2021clam], but no direct comparator is available
for multimodal RNA-Seq and WSI fusion under matched input
conditions.

| Metric | Value |
| :--- | :---: |
| ROC-AUC | 0.8482 |
| ROC-AUC (95% CI, DeLong) | 0.787 to 0.910 |
| ROC-AUC gain over late fusion baseline | +0.0801 |
| ROC-AUC gain over best unimodal baseline (ABMIL) | +0.1388 |
| PR-AUC at 2:1 class imbalance | 0.9054 |
| Brier Score | 0.17 |

: Key results on the 191-patient held-out cohort. {#tbl-key-results}

![ROC and Precision-Recall curves for the cross-attention + gate
model on the 191-patient held-out
cohort.](reports/figures/roc_pr_curves.png){#fig-roc
fig-alt="ROC and PR curves for the cross-attention + gate model."}

### Cross-Modal Reliability Evaluation {#sec-architectural-evolution}

The Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator is trained using a direction
anchor loss that ties the confidence score α directly to cosine
similarity between the visual embedding v and transcriptomic
query g. Standard BCE loss alone produced global threshold
collapse; the gate shifted α uniformly rather than
discriminating between patients. The anchor loss resolves this
by supervising α against cross-modal agreement:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}} = \text{MSE}\!\left(\alpha,\;
\sigma(s \cdot \text{cos}(v, g))\right)$$

High α indicates the two streams agree; low α indicates
discordance. CHIEF ViT-B visual embeddings and RNA-Seq
projections are nearly orthogonal in this cohort (cosine
similarity mean = -0.032), requiring a sharpening factor
s = 20 to spread anchor targets away from 0.5.

Following anchor loss training and Platt calibration, the
estimator produces a directionally stable, class-imbalance-robust
per-patient concordance signal (balanced p = 1.02e-09, verified
on a class-balanced subsample). The calibrated flagging threshold
is approximately 0.75 to 0.80.

### Survival Analysis {#sec-survival-analysis}

To test whether the fused representation carries prognostic
information beyond PR-status classification, a Cox
proportional-hazards layer was added to the cross-attention
architecture and evaluated for overall survival (OS) on the
held-out cohort (187 patients with usable OS data, 18 events).

The multimodal Cox model achieved a concordance index of
C-index = 0.780, compared to 0.700 for a clinical-only
baseline (age and AJCC stage) and 0.648 for a unimodal WSI
model (ABMIL encoder). This ordering is directional only:
with 18 events, bootstrap 95% confidence intervals overlap
substantially across all three models, and no claim of
statistical superiority is warranted.

### Interpretability Analysis {#sec-interpretability}

Analysis of attention patterns using the Top-1%-Mass Concentration
metric reveals significantly higher attentional focus in PR- patients
than PR+ patients (p = 0.018), consistent with the focal
architectural abnormalities characteristic of hormone
receptor-negative disease [@elston1991grading], as shown in
@fig-concentration. The entropy-based metric yields p = 0.401 on
the same data, confirming the signal was suppressed by the
slide-size confounder rather than absent from the model.

![Top-1%-Mass Concentration (mean ± SEM) by PR status. PR- patients
show significantly higher focal attention concentration (p = 0.018).
The entropy-based metric yielded p = 0.401 on the same data,
attributable entirely to the slide-size
confound.](reports/figures/concentration_bar.png){#fig-concentration
fig-alt="Bar chart of Top-1% mass concentration by PR status."
width=60%}

## Biological Interpretation {#sec-biological-interpretation}

### Attention Patterns and PR Phenotype {#sec-focal-distributed}

The Top-1%-Mass Concentration analysis reveals a significant difference
in attention distribution between PR-negative and PR-positive tumors
(p = 0.018). PR-negative patients exhibit higher concentration than
PR-positive patients (0.0888 vs 0.0705), indicating that the model
selectively focuses on a smaller subset of tissue regions when
classifying hormone receptor-negative disease.

This pattern is consistent with known histopathologic differences
between PR phenotypes. PR-negative tumors are more frequently
associated with higher-grade morphological features, including
increased mitotic activity, geographic necrosis, and pushing borders
[@elston1991grading], whereas PR-positive tumors more commonly exhibit
organized glandular architecture characteristic of luminal disease.
The model was not provided explicit supervision for these structures;
the observed attention patterns therefore suggest that transcriptomic
conditioning enables retrieval of morphologically informative regions
associated with PR status.

Attention spotlight maps provide qualitative evidence of this spatial
behavior, showing distributed tissue interrogation in PR-positive cases
and more focal attention patterns in PR-negative cases
(@fig-spotlight-map). These findings demonstrate that appropriate
normalization of attention measurements can reveal biologically
associated spatial patterns that are obscured by slide-size-dependent
metrics such as entropy.

![Attention Spotlight Maps. PR+ case (left): distributed attention
survey. PR- case (right): focal attention spotlighting. White
contours represent the
top 1% attention mass
boundary.](reports/figures/attention_spotlight_map.png){#fig-spotlight-map
fig-alt="Side-by-side spotlight maps for PR+ and PR- cases showing
attention concentration."}

### Borderline IHC Cases {#sec-borderline-cases}

The Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator is designed to flag cases
where transcriptomic and imaging evidence disagree, illustrating a
potential mechanism for selective escalation to pathologist review.
On the 191-patient held-out cohort, the gate demonstrates the intended
directional behavior: among concordant cases (calibrated α > 0.75), 83.1%
are PR+; among flagged cases (α < 0.75), 67.2% are PR-, as
shown in @tbl-gate-distribution.

| | Concordant (α > 0.75) | Flagged for review (α < 0.75) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| PR+ | 108 (83.1%) | 20 (32.8%) |
| PR- | 22 (16.9%) | 41 (67.2%) |
| **Total** | **130** | **61** |

: Gate concordance distribution across the 191-patient held-out
cohort. Column percentages within each confidence band.
{#tbl-gate-distribution}

The gate separates classes in both directions, demonstrating
the expected directional separation. The current escalation rate of
31.9%, meaning roughly one in three patients would be routed to
pathologist review, is higher than the 5 to 15% range typically
considered actionable for clinical triage tools. The near-orthogonal
embedding alignment between CHIEF ViT-B and RNA-Seq projections
(cosine similarity mean = -0.032) is the hypothesized contributor;
replacing the visual encoder with a transcriptomically-guided
alternative such as TITAN is the prescribed next step to test
this hypothesis. Whether that change alone is sufficient to reach
an escalation rate suitable for clinical translation remains
an open empirical question.

The 22 PR- patients in the concordant band represent a separate
finding: cases where transcriptomic and imaging evidence agree
on a PR+ phenotype against the IHC label. These are potential
IHC errors where the binary read-out may have suppressed partial
or heterogeneous receptor expression near the positivity
threshold, warranting quantitative H-score or Allred score
re-evaluation.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

Training and validation are confined to a single TCGA-BRCA cohort;
out-of-distribution performance is uncharacterized. The system
requires matched whole-transcriptome RNA-Seq data, which currently
involves greater cost and turnaround time than standard IHC
workflows. Top-1%-Mass Concentration measures where the model
concentrates capacity, not why; tissue processing artifacts can
dominate attention weight without biological basis. Spatial
relationships between tiles are not captured, which is acceptable
for PR-status classification but would be consequential for grading
or treatment response prediction. Cross-modal embedding alignment
is limited by the current visual encoder, pretrained on pathology
images alone; a transcriptomically-guided encoder is prescribed
for clinical translation. The survival and outcome associations
reported in this work are exploratory: the held-out cohort contains
only 18 observed events, and results at this scale require
validation in a larger cohort before any clinical interpretation.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This work introduces transcriptomics-conditioned visual search as a
framework for multimodal integration in computational pathology. By
treating the patient's RNA-Seq profile as a query that retrieves
diagnostically relevant regions from whole-slide images, the proposed
asymmetric cross-attention architecture addresses a fundamental
limitation of conventional fusion approaches: transcriptomic information is
used before visual compression rather than after.

On the TCGA-BRCA cohort of 951 patients, the model achieved an ROC-AUC
of 0.8482 and PR-AUC of 0.9054, outperforming unimodal and late-fusion
baselines under matched evaluation conditions. Beyond discrimination,
the Cross-Modal Reliability Estimator provides a patient-level signal
of genomic-imaging agreement, enabling selective identification of
cases requiring additional review. The proposed Top-1%-Mass Concentration
metric further demonstrates that reliable interpretation of attention
in variable-size whole-slide images requires normalization beyond
standard entropy-based measurements.

These findings suggest that effective multimodal pathology
systems require not only stronger fusion architectures but also
principled approaches for uncertainty estimation and
interpretation. Although external validation across institutions
and improved cross-modal encoders remain necessary before
clinical translation, the proposed framework is encoder-agnostic
and provides a general strategy for integrating molecular
profiles with high-resolution tissue imaging.

Several directions are prescribed for future work. External
validation on independent cohorts spanning multiple institutions,
staining protocols, and acquisition platforms is required before
clinical translation. Replacing the current visual encoder with
a transcriptomically-guided foundation model such as TITAN
[@chen2024titan] is the primary architectural next step, with
the hypothesis that stronger cross-modal alignment will improve
gate calibration and reduce the escalation rate to a range
suitable for clinical translation. Prospective evaluation of
the empirical flagging threshold (α < 0.75) against quantitative
H-score and Allred score outcomes in borderline IHC cases would
provide direct clinical validation of the reliability estimator.
Finally, region-level correlation between high-attention patches
and expert pathologist annotations would strengthen the
biological grounding of the Top-1%-Mass Concentration findings.
